title: The Wilson-Davis notes (2002)

lead.text: The Wilson-Davis notes are fifteen typed pages, dated 16 October 2002, in which Eric Davis, an AAWSAP contract author, records Vice Admiral Thomas Wilson describing how he was refused access to a special access programme holding recovered material in a contractor's custody. Davis says the notes are his and accurate; Wilson denies the meeting took place, and DoD witnesses asked about the memo in 2022 said they were unaware of it.

summary.text: The claim, as the notes record it: Wilson says that in 1997, as a senior intelligence officer, he tried to gain access to a programme holding recovered non-human material and was turned away on need-to-know grounds by a programme security officer, a contractor programme manager and a lawyer.

The document: typed notes headed as Eric Davis's meeting with Admiral Wilson, with a letter from a correspondent named Will Miller bound in as two of the pages; they surfaced in 2019 from private papers, not from any government release.

The people: Davis, earlier a NIDS scientist who worked under Harold Puthoff at EarthTech and now sits on the Sol Foundation's advisory board, was an AAWSAP contract author and says he later briefed Senate Armed Services staff and Senate Intelligence members on retrievals; Wilson was a former DIA director. The notes' account was raised with Pentagon witnesses at a 2022 hearing and is absent from AARO's 2024 history.

record.text: The copy in public circulation is fifteen typed pages headed EWD NOTES and dated 16 October 2002, numbered 1 to 15. Pages 3 and 4 are a two-page letter on Navy letterhead dated 25 April 2002, signed Will Miller and addressed to Davis as chief executive of Warp Drive Metrics, which the notes flag as a paper-clipped letter.

Miller's letter offers help with Davis's research into UFO crash retrievals and says that Miller once held top secret and compartmented clearances but no longer works in the classified realm. The notes give him no rank, service or first name beyond Will.
Read page by page, the published notes name Wilson, Davis, Steven Greer, Will Miller and Edgar Mitchell; Brig. Gen. Steven Lovekin, often linked to them, does not appear.
At the House Intelligence subcommittee hearing of 17 May 2022, the DoD witnesses Ronald Moultrie and Scott Bray were asked about the Wilson-Davis memo and said they were unaware of it.

AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I contains no occurrence of the names Wilson or Davis in its 63 pages, although it records a senior military officer's account of a craft in a building kept outside government so the technology could stay proprietary.

Davis's official output is on record: DIA listed him to the Senate Armed Services Committee as author of five of the 38 AAWSAP reference documents, and the released cover of one names him, of EarthTech International, as its author under DIA's programme. His antigravity survey concludes that each proposed device faces daunting technical challenges.

claimed.text: The notes record Wilson confirming that Greer, Miller and Mitchell gave a talk in a Pentagon conference room in April 1997, and that afterwards Miller and Wilson talked privately for two hours about UFOs, MJ-12, Roswell and crashed craft.

The chain by which the notes say the account travelled runs through three people: Wilson was angry that Miller had repeated their conversation, and Davis's own note says Miller told Edgar Mitchell, who told Davis only in 1999.

Davis has confirmed to journalists that the notes are his. On a podcast in March 2026 he said they are real and 100 percent accurate, that the circulating copy is a typewritten version of a handwritten one, and that it came from Mitchell's estate, while saying he could not confirm or deny that he and Wilson met.
A later report places the meeting at an EG&G facility in Las Vegas; the board holds that at Tier 3.

Davis told the New York Times in 2020 that he had briefed Senate Armed Services staff and Senate Intelligence members in October 2019 on retrievals of unexplained objects, and a Defense Department agency in March 2020 about retrievals from off-world vehicles not made on this earth, and said of the materials that we couldn't make it ourselves; the paper identified him as working for the Aerospace Corporation at the time.

On the board's reading, the refusal the notes describe, with security officers and contractor gatekeepers denying a cleared senior official, matches the mechanism David Grusch described under oath in 2023; that is an inference, not corroboration.

contested.text: Thomas Wilson denies that the meeting took place and denies the substance attributed to him. His denial and Davis's confirmation cannot both be true, and no agency has tried to resolve them.

An author endorsing his own notes is not authentication: Davis vouches for the text while declining to confirm the meeting, and the DoD witnesses asked about the memo in 2022 said they were unaware of it.

The record disagrees on the document's form and route. It is widely described as handwritten, while the published copy is typed; one account says it surfaced from Edgar Mitchell's estate, another that its pages left Kit Green's holdings, with Green not vouching for their contents.
Details common in retellings are not in the document: the form Cdr. Willard Miller, USN is unsupported by the notes, and Lovekin is not named in them.

AARO does not engage the notes, but attributes the claim that the government reverse-engineers extraterrestrial technology largely to circular reporting among believers, and says executives of the companies interviewees named denied such programmes on the record.

An earlier Senate inquiry reached EG&G and stopped: Richard D'Amato's public statement is that 1940s crash allegations did not merit further investigation, while George Knapp attributes to him a private view that a cover-up inside a company such as Lockheed Martin or EG&G was entirely feasible.
The skeptic Brian Dunning calls the Wilson-Davis memo an obviously hoaxed document, in itemising the claims of Jason Sands, who treats it as genuine.

questions: Where did the notes go between 2002 and 2019, and did they reach the public from Mitchell's estate, from Kit Green's holdings, or both?
Does the handwritten version Davis mentions exist, and does it match the typed copy?
Did the meeting take place, and where? The EG&G venue rests on a single later report.
Who is Will Miller, what was his service, and what did he tell Mitchell about his 1997 conversation with Wilson?
Why did AARO's historical review not address the notes, and will its promised second volume?
Do Senate committee files hold any record of Davis's October 2019 briefings?
